what_its_for: Epoetin alfa-epbx is used to treat anemia, which means you do not have enough red blood cells. It works by telling your body to make more red blood cells. It is used in people with chronic kidney disease (whether or not you are on dialysis), people receiving chemotherapy for certain cancers, and people taking zidovudine (AZT) for HIV infection. It may also be used before certain surgeries to reduce the need for blood transfusions.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous) or into a vein (intravenous). Your doctor or nurse will show you how to give the injection at home if needed. Always use a new, sterile needle and syringe each time. Inject under the skin in the outer area of your upper arm, thigh, or stomach area — but NOT near your belly button. Do not shake the vial. Check the liquid before use — it should be clear and colorless. Do not use if it looks cloudy, discolored, or has particles in it. Never reuse needles or syringes. Dispose of used needles in a puncture-resistant sharps container right away.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your condition, lab results (especially hemoglobin levels), and how you respond to the medicine. The dose is not the same for everyone. Never change your dose on your own without talking to your doctor. Your doctor will do regular blood tests to check your hemoglobin levels and adjust your dose to use the lowest dose that works for you. The goal is to keep your hemoglobin at the level your doctor recommends — usually no higher than 11 g/dL.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, give it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not give two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze. If the medicine accidentally freezes, do not use it. Keep it in the original carton to protect it from light. Do not leave it at room temperature for more than 24 hours total. Once a single-use vial has been opened, use it right away and throw away any leftover medicine — do not save it for later. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Avoid driving or using heavy machinery if you feel dizzy or confused, especially when you first start this medicine. Do not start this medication if you have uncontrolled high blood pressure — tell your doctor before starting. Avoid missing your blood pressure medications, as this drug can raise blood pressure. Do not use if you have cancer and your doctor has not specifically prescribed it for chemotherapy-related anemia. Avoid skipping your regular blood test appointments — these are important to make sure the medicine is working safely.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor RIGHT AWAY or go to the emergency room if you experience: sudden chest pain, shortness of breath, or trouble breathing; sudden numbness or weakness on one side of your body, sudden confusion, trouble speaking, or vision changes (possible signs of stroke); sudden severe headache; pain, swelling, or redness in your leg (possible blood clot); signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing; seizures; or a significant increase in your blood pressure. Also call your doctor if you feel very tired and the medicine does not seem to be helping, or if you notice any new or unusual symptoms.
when_it_works: Epoetin alfa-epbx does not work overnight. It usually takes 2 to 6 weeks of regular treatment before your red blood cell count starts to go up and you begin to feel less tired. Some people may take longer to notice a difference. Your doctor will check your blood regularly to see how well the medicine is working. Do not stop using it without talking to your doctor, even if you feel better.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Use only if your doctor decides the benefit outweighs the risk. Kidney disease: Your doctor will adjust your dose carefully and monitor you closely. Children: This medicine can be used in children in certain situations; your child's doctor will determine the appropriate dose. Older adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects such as high blood pressure and blood clots — your doctor will monitor you closely. Cancer patients: This medicine is only appropriate for anemia caused by chemotherapy; it is not for all cancer-related anemia and may increase the risk of tumor growth or blood clots in some situations — discuss the risks and benefits with your doctor.
